26186: A fragmentary letter of the emperor Claudius carved on stone at Delphi names 'Junius Gallio, my friend and proconsul'. It is dated by Claudius' 26th acclamation as emperor, which falls in AD 52, placing Gallio's proconsulship around AD 51–52.
26187: The Gallio (Delphi) inscription, published by É. Bourguet and later A. Plassart; text in Dittenberger, Sylloge Inscriptionum Graecarum (3rd ed.) 801
26188: Seneca's letters say Gallio caught a fever in Achaia and took a sea voyage for his health.
26190: Tacitus records that Gallio was frightened for his life after Seneca's death following the Pisonian conspiracy; later sources say he too died by suicide.
26192: Cool, legal and a little bored; a cultivated Roman who wants facts that fit the law and has no patience for theology.
26195: ruler of the synagogue in Corinth
26198: Crispus, the ruler of the synagogue, believed in the Lord together with his whole household, and many Corinthians believed and were baptized.
26200: Paul later recalls that Crispus was one of only a few people in Corinth he baptized personally.
26201: Crispus was the ruler of the synagogue in Corinth, the leader responsible for its services. He and his whole household believed in Jesus after Paul's preaching, and Paul baptized him personally. His conversion was a striking sign that the gospel could win respected leaders of the Jewish community.
26202: Acts and 1 Corinthians independently mention him (Acts 18:8; 1 Cor 1:14), one of several points where Acts and Paul's letters match.
26203: Dignified and thoughtful, a synagogue official who weighs scripture carefully before committing.
26206: co-sender of 1 Corinthians (if the same man)
26208: After Gallio dismissed the case against Paul, the crowd seized Sosthenes, the synagogue ruler, and beat him in front of the tribunal.
26210: Paul opens 1 Corinthians, written from Ephesus, in the name of himself and 'our brother Sosthenes'.
26211: Acts names Sosthenes as the ruler of the synagogue in Corinth who was beaten in front of the governor Gallio after the case against Paul collapsed. A Sosthenes also appears as 'our brother' alongside Paul at the start of 1 Corinthians. Whether these are the same man, later converted, is debated.
26212: Acts does not say who beat him or why (Acts 18:17); some manuscripts add that it was 'the Greeks'. 1 Corinthians calls a Sosthenes 'our brother' (1 Cor 1:1).
26214: Many readers think the synagogue ruler later believed and joined Paul, which would explain why Corinthians knew him. Others note that Sosthenes was a common name and think the link is only possible.
26216: If Gentile onlookers beat him, it may show anti-Jewish feeling in Corinth; if fellow Jews, they may have blamed him for a failed prosecution or suspected he sympathised with Paul.
26217: Later lists count Sosthenes among the seventy disciples sent out by Jesus.
26219: Sober and bruised but steady; a man who has paid a price for standing near Paul.
26226: From Ephesus Paul sent two of his helpers, Timothy and Erastus, ahead into Macedonia.
26228: In Romans, written from Corinth, Paul passes on greetings from 'Erastus, the city treasurer'.
26230: Near the end of 2 Timothy, Paul notes that Erastus remained at Corinth.
26231: Erastus was a co-worker of Paul connected with Corinth. Acts mentions him as a helper sent to Macedonia, Romans calls an Erastus the city treasurer (or city steward) of Corinth, and 2 Timothy says he stayed in Corinth. These may all be the same man, though that is not certain. A Latin inscription on a paving stone in Corinth names an Erastus who paid for the pavement in return for his office as aedile, a city official; whether he is Paul's Erastus is much debated.
26232: Romans 16:23 uses the Greek word oikonomos, 'manager' or 'steward' of the city. It does not say whether this was a senior office or a lower administrative post.
26234: Many identify the helper of Acts 19:22 and 2 Tim 4:20 with the treasurer of Rom 16:23; others think a city official would not be free to travel as Paul's helper and see two men.
26236: Some scholars identify the aedile of the inscription with Paul's Erastus, which would mean a wealthy, high-status convert in Corinth. Others argue that oikonomos is not the Greek for aedile, that Erastus was a fairly common name, and that the inscription may date from the later first or even second century. The question is unresolved.
26237: A paving inscription found near the theatre at Corinth in 1929 reads, in Latin, that Erastus laid the pavement at his own expense in return for his aedileship. Its date (mid-first century or later) and its link to the New Testament Erastus are debated.
26238: Corinth Erastus inscription (Corinth VIII.3, no. 232; discussed by J. H. Kent 1966 and S. J. Friesen 2010)
26239: Later Greek tradition counts Erastus among the Seventy and makes him a bishop.
26240: Later lists of the Seventy (needs verification)
26241: Practical and well-organised, at home with accounts and civic business, quietly generous.
26245: From the Roman province of Asia (western Turkey)
26248: church representative with the collection for Jerusalem
26250: Tychicus, from Asia, was one of the companions who went with Paul from Greece through Macedonia to Troas, probably as a delegate carrying the churches' gift for Jerusalem.
26252: Paul calls him a beloved brother, faithful minister and fellow servant, and sends him with Onesimus to tell the Colossians all Paul's news and encourage them.
26254: Ephesians also names Tychicus as the one who will bring news of Paul and encourage the readers.
26255: Possible replacement for Titus in Crete
26256: Paul tells Titus that when he sends Artemas or Tychicus, Titus should come to him at Nicopolis.
26258: In Paul's last letter he says, 'Tychicus I have sent to Ephesus.'
26259: Joins Paul's party leaving Greece through Macedonia.
26260: Goes ahead and waits for Paul at Troas.
26261: With Paul during his imprisonment (Rome is the traditional location; Ephesus and Caesarea are also proposed).
26262: Carries Colossians (and probably Philemon) with Onesimus.
26263: Named as the bearer of news to the Ephesians.
26264: Possibly sent to relieve Titus in Crete.
26265: Sent to Ephesus during Paul's final imprisonment.
26266: Tychicus was one of Paul's most trusted messengers, a believer from the province of Asia. He travelled with Paul toward Jerusalem with the collection for the poor, and during Paul's imprisonment he carried letters and news to the churches at Colossae and Ephesus. Paul repeatedly calls him a beloved brother and faithful minister, and his name appears in Paul's final letters as someone Paul could send wherever he was needed.
26267: Colossians and Ephesians describe his role in almost identical words (Col 4:7-8; Eph 6:21-22), a link scholars use when discussing how the two letters are related.
26269: Ancient letters were often carried by a trusted person who could explain and add to them in person; many think Tychicus played that role.
26271: Scholars who think Ephesians, Colossians or the Pastoral Letters were written after Paul's death read Tychicus' appearances as part of the letters' framing; those who hold Pauline authorship read them as real travel notes.
26272: Dependable and discreet; speaks like a trusted courier who has news to share and knows how to share it gently.
26280: delegate from Asia with the collection
26282: Trophimus, from Asia, was among the companions who went ahead of Paul to Troas.
26284: Jews from Asia had seen Trophimus the Ephesian with Paul in Jerusalem and wrongly assumed Paul had brought him, a Gentile, into the temple. The accusation set off the riot that led to Paul's arrest.
26286: Paul writes that he left Trophimus ill at Miletus.
26287: His home city; Acts calls him 'the Ephesian'.
26288: Goes ahead of Paul and waits at Troas.
26289: Seen with Paul in the city, sparking the false charge of temple defilement.
26290: Left behind sick on a later journey.
26291: Trophimus was a Gentile believer from Ephesus who travelled with Paul to Jerusalem, probably as a delegate carrying the churches' gift for the poor. Because people had seen him with Paul in the city, Paul was falsely accused of bringing a Gentile into the inner temple courts, which led to a riot and Paul's arrest. Later Paul mentions leaving him sick at Miletus.
26292: Acts says the crowd 'supposed' Paul had brought Trophimus into the temple (Acts 21:29); it never says he did. Gentiles were forbidden, on pain of death, to pass the barrier into the inner courts.
26294: His being 'left sick' (2 Tim 4:20) is often noted in discussions of healing: even Paul's close companions were not always healed.
26296: Two Greek warning inscriptions from the temple barrier have been found, forbidding foreigners to enter on pain of death, which illustrates the charge in Acts 21:28.
26297: Earnest and a little rueful; a Gentile believer acutely aware of what his presence once cost his friend.
26301: founder of the church at Colossae (probably)
26305: Paul says the Colossians learned the gospel from Epaphras, 'our beloved fellow servant', who had reported their love in the Spirit to Paul.
26307: Epaphras, 'one of you', was always struggling in prayer for the Colossians to stand mature, and had worked hard for the believers in Laodicea and Hierapolis.
26309: Paul calls him 'my fellow prisoner in Christ Jesus'.
26310: Epaphras was a believer from Colossae who appears to have brought the gospel to his home town and to nearby Laodicea and Hierapolis, probably while Paul was based in Ephesus. He later joined Paul during his imprisonment, bringing news of the Colossian church, and Paul describes him as a faithful minister who wrestled in prayer for his people.
26311: Paul never visited Colossae himself (Col 2:1); he credits Epaphras with teaching them (Col 1:7). Philemon calls him a fellow prisoner (Phlm 1:23), which may mean literal imprisonment or voluntary sharing of Paul's confinement.
26313: Epaphras is a short form of Epaphroditus, but most scholars think the two are different men: Epaphras is linked with Colossae, Epaphroditus with Philippi.
26314: Intense and pastoral, constantly bringing names before God; talks about his congregation like a worried, devoted father.
26317: If Philippians was written from Ephesus
26321: Paul thanks the Philippians for the gifts sent through Epaphroditus, calling them a fragrant offering acceptable to God.
26323: Epaphroditus fell so ill that he nearly died, but God had mercy on him and on Paul.
26325: Paul sends him back, probably carrying the letter, and tells the church to honour such men because he risked his life for the work of Christ.
26326: Sent by the Philippian church with their gift for Paul.
26327: Reaches Paul in prison and falls gravely ill. Rome is the traditional setting; Ephesus and Caesarea are also proposed.
26328: Returns home, probably carrying the letter to the Philippians.
26329: Epaphroditus was a member of the church at Philippi whom the believers sent to bring Paul a gift and to help him while he was in prison. While with Paul he became so sick that he almost died, and he was distressed that his home church had heard. Paul sent him home with the letter to the Philippians, calling him 'my brother, fellow worker and fellow soldier' and urging the church to honour him.
26330: Paul calls him the Philippians' 'messenger', using the Greek word apostolos in its ordinary sense of 'someone sent' (Phil 2:25). Paul does not say he was healed by a miracle, only that 'God had mercy on him' (Phil 2:27).
26332: Traditionally Philippians is placed in Rome around AD 61–62; some scholars argue for Ephesus around AD 55 because of the several journeys implied between Philippi and Paul's prison.
26333: Selfless and a little embarrassed by attention, more worried about others' anxiety than his own near-death.
26336: Paul's co-worker who later left him
26338: Demas sends greetings with Mark, Aristarchus and Luke, and Paul calls them all his fellow workers (also Col 4:14).
26340: In Paul's last letter he writes that Demas, 'in love with this present world', has deserted him and gone to Thessalonica.
26341: Demas was one of Paul's fellow workers during his imprisonment, named alongside Luke in Colossians and Philemon. In 2 Timothy, Paul sadly reports that Demas has abandoned him because he loved 'this present world' and has gone to Thessalonica. He has become a byword for a promising helper who did not finish well.
26342: Paul does not say what 'loving this present world' meant in practice, or whether Demas left the faith or only left Paul's dangerous situation (2 Tim 4:10).
26344: Some read his departure as giving up the faith; others think he simply fled the danger of Paul's final imprisonment and may have kept serving elsewhere.
26345: Capable and friendly but restless; he speaks of safer prospects and practical reasons.
26348: minister in the church at Colossae
26350: Greeted in the letter to Philemon
26351: Paul addresses Philemon, Apphia and 'Archippus our fellow soldier', and the church meeting in their house.
26353: Paul asks the Colossians to tell Archippus: 'See that you fulfil the ministry you have received in the Lord.'
26354: Archippus was a believer at Colossae whom Paul calls his 'fellow soldier'. He is greeted along with Philemon and Apphia, and Colossians gives him a public charge to complete the ministry the Lord had given him. Because he is named with Philemon and Apphia, many think he was part of their household, perhaps their son.
26355: Scripture does not say what his ministry was, or whether the reminder in Col 4:17 was encouragement or gentle correction.
26357: A common suggestion is that Archippus was Philemon's son; this is a guess from the order of names (Phlm 1:1-2).
26359: John Knox (the 20th-century scholar) proposed that Archippus, not Philemon, owned Onesimus, and that Archippus' 'ministry' was to release him. Most scholars have not accepted this.
26360: Earnest and a little burdened by responsibility, aware that a whole church is watching him.
26364: Macedonian, from Thessalonica; Jewish by birth (Col 4:10-11)
26367: During the riot stirred up by Demetrius, the crowd dragged Gaius and Aristarchus, Macedonian travelling companions of Paul, into the theatre.
26369: Aristarchus of Thessalonica was among those who travelled with Paul as he left Greece for Jerusalem.
26371: When Paul was sent as a prisoner to Rome, Aristarchus, a Macedonian from Thessalonica, went with him and so shared the storm and shipwreck.
26373: Paul calls him 'my fellow prisoner' and names him among the few Jewish co-workers who had been a comfort to him (Col 4:10-11; Phlm 1:24).
26375: Caught up in the silversmiths' riot.
26376: Travels with Paul's party on the way to Jerusalem.
26377: Boards the ship with the prisoner Paul.
26378: With the ship as it shelters on Crete before the storm.
26379: Shipwrecked with all on board (Acts' 'we' includes Paul's companions).
26380: With Paul during his imprisonment and named as a fellow prisoner.
26381: Aristarchus was a Jewish believer from Thessalonica in Macedonia and one of Paul's most loyal companions. He was dragged into the theatre during the riot at Ephesus, travelled with Paul to Jerusalem, and later sailed with him as a prisoner to Rome, surviving storm and shipwreck. Paul calls him a fellow prisoner and a comfort.
26382: Acts names him three times (Acts 19:29; Acts 20:4; Acts 27:2). In Colossians he is 'my fellow prisoner' (Col 4:10), while in Philemon he is a 'fellow worker' (Phlm 1:24).
26383: Why did he sail with Paul?
26384: Some think he travelled as Paul's servant or friend so that the prisoner could have help; others think he was simply heading home to Macedonia on the first ship and then chose to go on to Rome.
26385: Steady and loyal, a man of few words who has been through riots and shipwrecks and speaks of them calmly.
26392: host of Paul and the church at Corinth
26396: Paul says he personally baptized only Crispus and Gaius among the Corinthians (and Stephanas' household).
26397: Host to Paul and the whole church
26398: Writing from Corinth, Paul sends greetings from 'Gaius, who is host to me and to the whole church'.
26399: Dragged into the theatre at Ephesus
26400: A Macedonian Gaius was seized with Aristarchus in the Ephesus riot.
26401: Gaius of Derbe travels with Paul
26402: A Gaius of Derbe is listed among Paul's companions on the way to Jerusalem.
26404: The elder writes to his beloved Gaius, praising him for walking in the truth and welcoming travelling teachers.
26405: Gaius was one of the most common Roman first names, and the New Testament mentions at least three or four believers called Gaius. One lived in Corinth, was baptized by Paul and hosted the whole church in his house. Another, from Macedonia, was seized in the riot at Ephesus, and a Gaius from Derbe travelled with Paul to Jerusalem. The short letter of 3 John is addressed to a Gaius praised for his hospitality. This entry gathers them, since the texts do not let us be sure how many different people are meant.
26406: Each passage gives a different identifier: Corinth (1 Cor 1:14; Rom 16:23), Macedonia (Acts 19:29), Derbe (Acts 20:4), and the unnamed setting of 3 John (3 John 1:1).
26408: Most scholars think at least three different people are meant. Some identify Gaius of Corinth with 'Titius Justus' of Acts 18:7, giving him the full Roman name Gaius Titius Justus; this is an attractive but unproven suggestion.
26410: Nothing ties the Gaius of 3 John to the others; he is usually placed in the province of Asia late in the first century.
26411: The Apostolic Constitutions say the apostle John appointed a Gaius as bishop of Pergamum. The source is late (4th century).
26413: Generous and open-handed, a host who measures faith by an open door and a ready table.
26416: controlling leader in a local church
26417: Rejects the elder and his messengers
26418: Diotrephes, 'who loves to be first', refused to accept the elder's authority, spread malicious talk about him, would not welcome travelling believers, and put out of the church those who did.
26419: Diotrephes was a leader in a local church who, according to the short letter of 3 John, loved to be first. He refused to welcome the author ('the elder') or the travelling teachers the elder sent, spoke against him, and expelled church members who showed them hospitality. The elder promises to deal with him in person.
26420: 3 John describes him only from the elder's side (3 John 1:9-10). It does not accuse him of false teaching, only of pride, slander and refusing hospitality.
26422: Many scholars see an early clash between travelling leadership (like the elder's messengers) and an emerging single local leader or bishop.
26424: Tradition identifies the elder with John the apostle; many scholars think he was a different leader, sometimes called John the Elder. The identification is debated.
26425: Domineering and suspicious, protective of his own position, quick to call outsiders troublemakers.
26428: commended believer, probably the bearer of 3 John
26430: The elder says that Demetrius has a good report from everyone and from the truth itself, and adds his own testimony.
26431: Demetrius is a believer warmly recommended in 3 John. Everyone speaks well of him, and the elder adds his own endorsement. He may have carried the letter to Gaius, and the recommendation stands in deliberate contrast to the proud Diotrephes.
26432: 3 John gives a threefold witness to him: from everyone, from the truth, and from the elder (3 John 1:12).
26434: A few have suggested he was the Ephesian silversmith converted; there is no evidence for this and most scholars treat them as different people.
26435: Quiet and trustworthy, letting his reputation speak for him.
26441: Paul reminds Timothy of the sincere faith that lived first in his grandmother Lois and his mother Eunice, and now in him.
26442: Lois was Timothy's grandmother, the mother of Eunice. Paul praises the sincere faith that lived first in her, then in her daughter, and then in Timothy. She is a picture of how faith and scripture are handed down in a family.
26443: Scripture names her only once (2 Tim 1:5). Timothy had known the holy scriptures from childhood (2 Tim 3:15), probably through Lois and Eunice.
26445: Some think 'faith' here refers to her Jewish faith before she knew of Jesus; others think she became a believer in Jesus, perhaps during Paul's first visit to Lystra (Acts 14:6-7).
26446: Gentle and steady, quoting the scriptures she taught her grandson at her knee.
26453: At Lystra Paul met Timothy, 'the son of a Jewish woman who was a believer, but his father was a Greek', and took him on as a co-worker.
26455: Paul names Eunice with her mother Lois as the source of Timothy's sincere faith.
26456: Eunice was Timothy's mother, a Jewish believer in Jesus married to a Greek man. Acts mentions her without naming her, and 2 Timothy names her alongside her own mother Lois as a woman of sincere faith who taught Timothy the scriptures from childhood.
26457: Acts calls her a 'believer' (Acts 16:1). Because Timothy had not been circumcised as a child (Acts 16:3), many infer that her Greek husband's wishes prevailed at home, though the text does not say so.
26458: Warm and resilient, a mother who held on to her faith in a mixed household and is quietly proud of her son.
26461: believer who sought out and refreshed the imprisoned Paul
26463: Onesiphorus was not ashamed of Paul's chains; when he came to Rome he searched hard for him until he found him, and often refreshed him.
26465: Paul reminds Timothy how much Onesiphorus had served at Ephesus, and later sends greetings to his household (2 Tim 4:19).
26466: Onesiphorus was a believer from Ephesus who, unlike many who deserted Paul, went looking for him in Rome during his final imprisonment and kept encouraging him. Paul prays that the Lord will show mercy to his household and to him 'on that day'.
26467: Paul prays for Onesiphorus' household (2 Tim 1:16; 2 Tim 4:19) and for Onesiphorus himself to find mercy on the day of judgement (2 Tim 1:18).
26469: Because Paul greets his household rather than him, many think Onesiphorus had died, and some cite the prayer for him as an early example of prayer for the dead.
26471: Many argue he may simply have been away from home, or that the prayer is a wish rather than an intercession for the dead; the text does not say he had died.
26472: Persistent and cheerful, the friend who keeps knocking on doors until he finds you.
